http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/18/qatar.text: Qatar said on Tuesday that an Iranian delegation travelled to Doha and collected the remains of one of its pilots, as Tehran continued to claim that three who went missing after their aircraft entered Qatari airspace and were shot down in March are still in the country.“The body was repatriated, and there was a funeral," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr Majed Al Ansari said in Doha, adding that Iran had not responded to Qatar’s invitation to send a technical team to review the search operation.“We have invited them to send a technical team so that they can review all the details of the search-and-rescue operation,” Al Ansari said.“Unfortunately, the Iranian side did not respond to this invitation.”An Iranian military official had earlier accused Qatar of preventing a fact-finding team from entering the country and called on the International Committee of the Red Cross to intervene.Qatar disputed that account and said its invitation remained open.“We are here, we are open,” Al Ansari said. “There is no need for media speculation in this case.”He called Iran’s accusations “false” and “illogical” and suggested they were aimed at an audience inside the country.“If the agenda is for domestic consumption to solve local issues, we are not concerned in that case,” he said.Al Ansari's comments came a day after Tehran said it would consider the three missing pilots to be prisoners until Qatar clarified their situation.Qatar denied holding the pilots in a statement on Saturday, saying it had contacted Iran to coordinate the handover of one pilot’s remains.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Tehran would pursue the case through bilateral, international and legal channels.What happened to the pilots?The pilots went missing after Iranian military aircraft entered Qatari airspace on 2 March, during the early days of the war that began with the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February.Tehran said the aircraft were taking part in an operation targeting the US Al Udeid Air Base when they were shot down by Qatari forces.Al Ansari said the aircraft had entered Qatari airspace and threatened people in the country.“These planes did not come here for leisure,” he said. “They came here to threaten the citizens and residents.”Qatar tried to contact the pilots but received no response before taking action to defend its territory, he added.Qatar says its search-and-rescue teams looked for the pilots following the 2 March incident and recovered the remains of one of them. Al Ansari said the search ended on 6 April.Qatar then contacted Iran to return the remains and invited an Iranian team to review the search details.“Instead of responding positively to this invitation, we were surprised by these statements,” Al Ansari said.Qatar says it will defend its territoryAl Ansari further said Doha would continue seeking a diplomatic solution to the ongoing war but would respond firmly to any future attack on the country.“Iran is not going anywhere, and we are not going anywhere,” he said. “We need to respect the sovereignty of countries, and each side should respect the other.”“Any attack against our state, we will face it firmly, and we will not hesitate to protect the people, the residents and our land.”He added that Qatar’s priority remained dialogue and a peaceful end to the crisis.Al Ansari also said there was no new progress to report in the Iran-Oman talks over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.Qatar was still waiting for the two countries to reach an agreement that could help restore the ceasefire and allow wider US-Iran negotiations to resume, he said.Asked how close the parties were to reviving the wider US-Iran agreement, Al Ansari said, “I think we are far from this right now.”He said an agreement to reopen Hormuz would make it easier for wider negotiations to move forward.

https://www.dw.com/en/uk-government-cond.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5M2Nc Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth following the arrival of about migrants who had crossed the English Channel from France Image: PA/PA Images/picture alliance Advertisement British minister Emma Reynolds on Monday slammed "thuggish" anti-migrant protests that blocked roads in the English coastal city of Portsmouth. Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday following the arrival of about 140 migrants who had crossed the English Channel from France, UK media reported. "This is thuggish and intimidating behavior," Reynolds, who is Chief Secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News, adding that the police brought the Portsmouth protest under control. The demonstration came a day after masked protesters disrupted traffic at Dover terminal, blocking routes to the busy ferry port. Masked protesters in Dover On Saturday, hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK. Video footage showed demonstrators, reportedly backed by far-right groups , in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English Channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Labour Party government said that "the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused." The Dover demonstration caused a traffic jam of about four miles (6.4 km) and temporarily halted traffic into and out of the port. Britain has struggled for years to curb small-boat crossings from France , although Reynolds said arrivals were down 43% from last year to about 17,000 so far this year. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Diesel prices have risen dramatically since the US war on Iran. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Diesel prices have risen dramatically since the US war on Iran. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images Trump administration Analysis Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say Simon Goodley Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’ Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.56 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.42 EDT Share Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted. The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran. The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration . “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted. However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections. Graph showing increase in price of US diesel US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon , according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday. Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small. “They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.” The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.” However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe . The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products. Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader” . On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output. “The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.” Explore more on these topics Trump administration US politics Energy industry Supply chain crisis Global economy International trade US economy analysis Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Coach services could be cut due to record diesel prices, UK operators warn Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speech UK diesel price hits record high of £2 a litre Italy PM Meloni ‘stunned’ by Trump’s claims she begged him for a photo Minister denies UK faces diesel shortage after Trump threatens to ban exports ‘Project Freedom’: a grand humanitarian gesture, or a fast track to more war? https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/1.text: Listen (2 mins) Save Share Russian attacks in Ukraine kill at least 8, cut power to 1 million on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google An emergency service deminer works at the site of an apartment building damaged during a Russian drone strike in the Rivne region, Ukraine, on October 16, 2026 [Handout/State Emergency Service of Ukraine via Reuters] By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters Published On 17 Oct 2026 17 Oct 2026 Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 across Ukraine, hit two shopping centres and cut power to more than a million people, Ukrainian officials have said. The attacks on Friday struck nine regions. In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man were killed and 12 people were wounded in strikes on three districts, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 ‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least 9, damages power sites list 2 of 3 Trump slams Zelenskyy as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries list 3 of 3 Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify end of list Two people were killed in Kramatorsk, a frontline city in the Donetsk region, and two more in the southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region. In the northwestern Volyn region, which borders Poland, a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight, Governor Roman Romaniuk said. Drones also hit a customs terminal and set fire to about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, on a major road from Kyiv to Poland . In Rivne, drones hit a major shopping centre and other sites, killing one person and wounding seven, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said. A shopping centre in Sumy, close to the front line, was also hit. Emergency service deminers work at the site of an apartment building damaged during a Russian drone strike in the Rivne region, Ukraine, on October 16, 2026 [Handout/State Emergency Service of Ukraine via Reuters] Power cuts Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy said repair crews had restored power to more than a million people who lost it on Friday. In Volyn, about 370,000 households lost power, with supply since restored to at least 100,000 of them. The blackout could last at least 24 hours in the regional capital, Lutsk, Mayor Andriy Razumovskyi said. Advertisement Large parts of Rivne were also left without power. Russia’s military chief told President Vladimir Putin on Friday that the military had allocated the assets needed to press its aerial campaign against Ukraine’s energy system. Civilian toll Meanwhile, the United Nations said on Friday that civilian casualties in Ukraine had climbed steeply. According to UN human rights monitors, at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded in Ukraine last month, 85 percent more than in September 2025. Between January and September 2026, 2,570 civilians were killed and 15,211 wounded, almost 60 percent more than in the same period last year and more than twice the 2024 level, the report said. “The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, head of the UN’s human rights monitoring mission in Ukraine.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/17/roma.text: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the Black Sea in the latest drone incident impacting the southeastern European nation, authorities said on Saturday.Defence Minister Radu Miruta said the first drone had entered Romanian airspace at around 17:59 and was shot down "within two minutes," 25 km south-east of the town of Sulina."The second drone, in the same area, was engaged and shot down at 18:05, five minutes after entering national airspace, 20 km east of Sulina," Miruta said.According to a Defence Ministry press release, two F-16s carrying out air policing missions were involved in the operation to intercept the drones after being scrambled from the 86th air base at Borcea, near the city of Fetești.The aircraft were called into action after radar surveillance systems detected a number of aerial targets, per the ministry. It later announced that the targets were "jet-powered attack drones from the Geran family.""The Black Sea serves as a critical maritime artery for the global export of grain, energy resources, and industrial commodities, making its stability vital to international food and energy security," Oana Toiu, Romania's foreign minister, wrote on X, adding that NATO would discuss Black Sea "defence and deterrence" at an upcoming meeting."The Black Sea will be safe again," she added.Sitting on NATO's eastern flank, Romania is particularly vulnerable to security threats stemming from Russia's war in Ukraine, and the country has been dealing with a surge in drone-related incursions and incidents believed to be linked to the conflict in recent months.
